idiom_name: #private field + guard methods; new Proxy(target, handler) for transparent or revocable guards
implementation_notes: The classic proxy/real-subject pair collapses into a single class: a #private field is 'private after compilation and does not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access' - 'the privacy encapsulation of these class elements is enforced by JavaScript itself' - so the resource cannot be named, enumerated or reached with bracket notation outside the defining class, and every public method is the authorize-then-delegate path. Where callers must keep using the resource's own API, the local idiom is new Proxy(target, handler): the get/set/apply traps authorize each operation and forward with Reflect, and Proxy.revocable() yields a handle that can be cut off later, the platform's own revocable capability. Neither is a security boundary against code in the same realm - the realm's globals can be patched before the guard is built and anyone holding the target bypasses the proxy - so a worker/process/server boundary is still needed for adversarial separation.
pitfalls: #private fields are not reachable through a Proxy: 'the proxy does not have direct access to the original object's private elements', so forwarding an object with #fields (or native objects with internal slots) through a proxy breaks - forward with the guard's own methods.

Trap invariants are enforced by the language: a trap that lies about a non-configurable property or a non-extensible target throws a TypeError instead of protecting anything, and self-referential Reflect calls inside a trap can recurse.

A guard in the same realm trusts the realm: module code can patch Reflect/global prototypes before the guard is constructed, and anyone holding the raw target skips the proxy - use a worker/process boundary when the threat model needs one.
A proxy has a different identity: ===, instanceof and WeakMap keys see the proxy, not the target, which breaks libraries that key state on object identity.

variants.name: Proxy trap front end (transparent, revocable)
variants.implementation_notes: When the resource's own API must stay usable, the guard becomes a handler: the get (and set/apply) trap consults the policy, then forwards through Reflect so the proxy keeps the internal-method semantics of the target, and the resource is stored in the handler's closure rather than on the exposed object. Proxy.revocable() adds the missing piece of a capability system - a revoke() that makes every later operation on the proxy fail, which is the JS analogue of withdrawing a handle. This is the realization to pick when the caller's code cannot be rewritten to a narrowed interface; the price is that identity (===, instanceof, WeakMap keys) now sees the proxy, and any code that obtains the target bypasses the handler.
pitfalls: The target is only protected while the handler holds it: any shared reference, closure capture or the revocable proxy pair's own target field hands the raw object to whoever can reach it.
revoke() invalidates the proxy, not operations already in flight: an async call that read the target before revocation continues against the resource.
Reflect used without the receiver (or with the wrong target) breaks getters/setters that rely on this; pass through Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver) exactly.
